stageDescription: What each framework addresses and when to reach for it.
title: Regulators: UK and India

stops.title: In one line
stops.contentMd:
## In one line

Neither the UK nor India has an EU-style AI law. Both rely on existing regulators applying shared principles, plus existing rules (consumer protection, model risk, data protection) to AI in their own sectors.

## Explained like you're 10

**The EU** wrote one big rulebook for every game in the school.

**The UK and India** said: "Here are our values: be fair, be safe, be honest." Then each sports coach applies them to their own sport. The swimming coach has swimming rules, the football coach has football rules. There's no single AI rulebook, so you have to know which coach is in charge of your game.

For a bank, the "coaches" are the financial regulators: the FCA and PRA in the UK, the RBI and SEBI in India. Their existing rules already apply to AI.

## Why they regulate differently from the EU

|  | EU | UK | India |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Model | One horizontal AI law | Principles applied by sector regulators | Guidelines; sector regulators lead |
| Philosophy | Protect rights through product-safety rules | Pro-innovation, avoid early lock-in | "Innovation over restraint" |
| Binding AI-specific rules | Yes, with fines | Few; mostly existing law applied to AI | Few; specific rules such as deepfake labelling |
| Where obligations come from | The AI Act | FCA, PRA, ICO, CMA rules and guidance | RBI, SEBI, MeitY rules, DPDP Act |

**What this means for a consultant:** for UK or Indian clients, you don't start with an AI law. You start with **"which regulators supervise this client, and what do their existing rules require when AI is involved?"** Then add the EU AI Act if they have EU exposure.

## Level 1: The UK approach

### The five principles (2023 white paper)

Safety, security and robustness; transparency and explainability; fairness; accountability and governance; contestability and redress. They aren't law; regulators apply them within their existing powers. As of mid-2026 there's still no general AI bill.

### Who does what

| Regulator | AI relevance |
| --- | --- |
| FCA (Financial Conduct Authority) | Applies existing rules to AI, especially the **Consumer Duty** (good customer outcomes) and **SM&CR** (named senior managers accountable). Runs an AI Lab and AI live-testing for firms. The FCA-commissioned [Mills Review](https://www.pwc.co.uk/industries/financial-services/understanding-regulatory-developments/fca-commissioned-review-sets-seven-point-ai-agenda-for-retail-finance.html) (July 2026) made seven recommendations, including clarifying how the Consumer Duty and SM&CR apply to more autonomous AI and preparing for agentic finance |
| PRA and Bank of England | **SS1/23** model risk management (see the Model risk tab); financial-stability work on AI, including agentic AI |
| ICO | UK GDPR; the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 reformed automated-decision rules; AI and data protection guidance |
| CMA | Competition in AI and foundation models |
| AI Security Institute | Government body testing advanced AI models; renamed from the AI Safety Institute in Feb 2025 |

**Interview line:** "In UK financial services, AI governance runs through the Consumer Duty, SM&CR and SS1/23. There's no AI Act, but a firm still has to show good outcomes, a named accountable senior manager and controlled models."

## Level 2: India's approach

India has chosen guidelines plus targeted rules, with sector regulators leading.

| Body or instrument | What to know |
| --- | --- |
| MeitY India AI Governance Guidelines (Nov 2025) | Seven sutras: trust is the foundation; people first; innovation over restraint; fairness and equity; accountability; understandable by design; safety, resilience and sustainability. No umbrella AI law. Proposes an AI Governance Group and a technology and policy expert committee, with the AI Safety Institute for technical work |
| IT Rules amendment (notified Feb 2026, effective 20 Feb 2026) | AI-generated ("synthetically generated") content must be **labelled** and carry provenance metadata; social media platforms must ask users to declare AI content; certain takedowns within **3 hours** |
| DPDP Act 2023 and Rules 2025 | Data protection; phased in from Nov 2025 (see the Privacy tab) |
| RBI | FREE-AI framework for banks and NBFCs (Level 3 below) |
| SEBI | Consultation (June 2025) proposing five areas for AI/ML in securities markets: model governance with senior-management accountability, disclosure to clients, testing and monitoring, fairness and bias, data privacy and security. Check whether final rules have been issued |
| CERT-In | Cyber incident reporting, which covers AI systems too |

**Interview line:** "India regulates AI through sector regulators and targeted rules, not one law. For a bank that means RBI's FREE-AI, the DPDP Act, and the 2026 deepfake labelling rules if it publishes AI-generated content."

## Level 3: RBI FREE-AI in depth

**FREE-AI** stands for Framework for Responsible and Ethical Enablement of AI. An RBI committee chaired by Prof. Pushpak Bhattacharyya (IIT Bombay) published it in August 2025. It is a set of **recommendations** for regulated entities (banks, NBFCs and others), not binding directions. Expect RBI to turn parts into guidance over time.

### Structure: 7 sutras, 6 pillars, 26 recommendations

The **7 sutras** are the same as MeitY's (above). The **6 pillars** split into two halves:

| Enable innovation | Mitigate risk |
| --- | --- |
| **Infrastructure:** shared data and compute, digital public infrastructure | **Governance:** board-approved AI policy, oversight structures |
| **Policy:** enabling regulation, an AI innovation sandbox | **Protection:** consumer protection, cybersecurity, incident reporting |
| **Capacity:** skills for boards, staff and supervisors | **Assurance:** a risk-based AI audit framework across the lifecycle |

### Recommendations a bank should act on

- A **board-approved AI policy**.
- A **risk-based audit framework** covering data inputs, model design, outputs and post-deployment monitoring.
- **Product approval** processes that cover higher-risk AI uses.
- **Consumer protection** measures for AI-driven services.
- **Cybersecurity and AI incident reporting**.
- Board and staff **capacity building** on AI.

**What a consultant does with it:** a gap assessment of an Indian bank against the 26 recommendations, mapped to an ISO 42001-style management system, so the bank is ready when RBI issues formal guidance.

## Level 4: Other jurisdictions to know

One line each is enough for most interviews.

| Jurisdiction | Approach |
| --- | --- |
| United States | No federal AI law. Federal policy shifted in 2025 towards deregulation (a new AI Action Plan in July 2025). States act alone: for example, New York City requires bias audits for automated hiring tools, and Colorado passed a broader AI Act whose start date has been pushed back. Sector regulators apply existing law, such as fair-lending rules |
| Singapore | Voluntary but influential: the Model AI Governance Framework, a GenAI framework (2024), and the AI Verify testing toolkit. For finance, MAS's FEAT principles: fairness, ethics, accountability, transparency |
| China | Binding rules for specific uses: recommendation algorithms, deep synthesis (deepfakes), generative AI services (2023), and mandatory labelling of AI-generated content (from Sept 2025). Algorithms registered with the regulator |
| International | OECD AI Principles, the G7 Hiroshima Process code of conduct, the Council of Europe's AI convention (the first international treaty on AI, 2024), UNESCO's Recommendation |

## Level 5: Advising a client across several jurisdictions

1. **Map the footprint:** where the client is based, where its customers are, where AI outputs are used, which regulators supervise it.
2. **Find the triggers:** the EU AI Act applies if outputs are used in the EU, even from India.
3. **Build one control set to the highest common standard,** with local additions. Don't run three separate programmes.
4. **Map each control to every framework** it satisfies (test once, comply many).
5. **Horizon scanning:** someone owns tracking regulatory change, reported to the AI committee quarterly.
6. **Watch for conflicts:** for example, data residency rules vs a vendor LLM hosted abroad.

**Interview line:** "For a multi-country client I'd build one AI control framework to the strictest common standard, usually EU-AI-Act-informed, with local overlays such as FREE-AI or the Consumer Duty, and map every control to each regime so the evidence is reusable."
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick a company you know (or a plausible one): where is it based, where are its customers, where might its AI outputs be 'used'? Map which of the regimes above (EU AI Act, UK principles/FCA/PRA, India FREE-AI/DPDP) would apply, and why.

stops.title: Worked example: an Indian bank with UK and EU customers
stops.contentMd:
## Worked example: an Indian bank with UK and EU customers

A fictional Mumbai-based bank, "Sindhu Bank", has a UK branch and an online lending app used by customers in Ireland. It uses an ML credit model and a customer chatbot.

| Regime | Triggered by | What it requires for the AI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RBI FREE-AI | Indian regulated entity | Board-approved AI policy, audit framework, incident reporting, consumer protection |
| DPDP Act | Indian customers' data | Consent or legitimate use; significant-data-fiduciary duties likely |
| IT Rules 2026 | Only if it publishes AI-generated audio or video | Labelling and provenance |
| FCA and PRA | UK branch | Consumer Duty outcomes, SM&CR accountability; SS1/23 if the branch's regime applies |
| UK GDPR | UK customers' data | Lawful basis, DPIA, automated-decision safeguards |
| EU AI Act | Credit model output used for Irish customers | Credit scoring is Annex III high-risk; FRIA; deployer or provider duties from Dec 2027. Chatbot needs Article 50 disclosure |
| GDPR | EU customers' data | Article 22 safeguards for automated credit decisions (SCHUFA) |

**Recommendation:** one AI policy and control library built to the EU AI Act standard for the credit model, with FREE-AI and Consumer Duty overlays, and a single combined impact assessment (DPIA, FRIA and AI impact assessment) per system.
stops.artifactPrompt: Using Sindhu Bank's method, pick a multi-jurisdiction company (real or hypothetical) and build the same table: which regime, what triggers it, what it requires. End with a one-line recommendation like the one above.

stops.title: Applied to your CV
stops.contentMd:
## Applied to your CV

You've worked under one regime and now sell into the other. That's rare, so say it.

| Experience | Use it as |
| --- | --- |
| Barclays UK: Consumer Duty, DISP, vulnerability guidance | Proof you know how UK financial regulators apply existing rules to AI |
| Barclays as an SS1/23 bank | You've worked inside a firm under formal model risk rules |
| Current work with BFSI clients in India | First-hand view of how Indian banks approach FREE-AI and DPDP |
| Moving from the UK to India | You can compare principles-based UK supervision with India's guideline-led approach |

**Interview line:** "I've seen AI governance from inside a UK bank under the Consumer Duty and SS1/23, and now from the Indian side, where banks are working out what FREE-AI and DPDP mean in practice. Neither has an AI Act, so the work is translating existing rules into AI controls."

## Free videos and courses

For regulators, primary documents are the best free material; no strong free video covering these was found.

| # | Resource | Source | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | RBI FREE-AI report | Reserve Bank of India | The full 26 recommendations |
| 2 | MeitY AI Governance Guidelines summary | S.S. Rana (law firm) | India's 7 sutras and institutions |
| 3 | Mills Review summary | PwC UK | Where UK financial AI regulation is heading |
stops.artifactPrompt: Write your own 'applied to your CV' row: name one piece of cross-jurisdiction or cross-regime experience you have (even informal), and one sentence on how you'd use it to answer an interview question.

stops.title: Interview questions
stops.contentMd:
## Interview questions

| Question | Crisp answer |
| --- | --- |
| How does the UK regulate AI? | No AI law. Five principles (safety, transparency, fairness, accountability, contestability) applied by existing regulators: FCA, PRA, ICO, CMA. |
| Which UK rules matter most for AI in banking? | Consumer Duty, SM&CR, PRA SS1/23, UK GDPR as amended in 2025. |
| What's the Mills Review? | An FCA-commissioned review (July 2026) with seven recommendations on AI in retail finance, including how the Consumer Duty and SM&CR apply to more autonomous AI. |
| How does India regulate AI? | Guidelines and sector regulators: MeitY's guidelines, RBI FREE-AI, SEBI proposals, the DPDP Act, and 2026 IT Rules on AI-generated content. |
| What is FREE-AI? | RBI's Aug 2025 framework: 7 sutras, 6 pillars, 26 recommendations, including a board-approved AI policy, AI audit framework and incident reporting. Recommendations, not yet binding directions. |
| Name the six FREE-AI pillars | Infrastructure, Policy, Capacity (enable innovation); Governance, Protection, Assurance (mitigate risk). |
| What did India's 2026 IT Rules change? | Mandatory labelling and provenance metadata for AI-generated content; certain takedowns within 3 hours. |
| Does the EU AI Act apply to an Indian bank? | If its AI outputs are used in the EU, such as scoring EU customers, yes. |
| How do you advise a client across regimes? | Map the footprint and triggers, build one control set to the highest common standard with local overlays, map controls to every regime, scan the horizon. |

quiz.question: How does the UK regulate AI?
quiz.answer: There's no AI law. Five principles — safety, transparency, fairness, accountability, contestability — are applied by existing regulators: FCA, PRA, ICO, CMA.
quiz.explanation: The UK's model is principles applied by sector regulators, not a horizontal AI statute.

quiz.question: Which UK rules matter most for AI in banking specifically?
quiz.answer: The Consumer Duty, SM&CR, PRA SS1/23, and UK GDPR as amended in 2025.
quiz.explanation: These four together cover customer outcomes, accountability, model risk, and data protection for AI in UK financial services.

quiz.question: What is the Mills Review?
quiz.answer: An FCA-commissioned review (July 2026) with seven recommendations on AI in retail finance, including clarifying how the Consumer Duty and SM&CR apply to more autonomous AI.
quiz.explanation: Shows you're current on where UK financial AI regulation is actually heading, not just the 2023 white paper.

quiz.question: How does India regulate AI?
quiz.answer: Through guidelines and sector regulators, not one law: MeitY's AI Governance Guidelines, RBI's FREE-AI, SEBI's proposals, the DPDP Act, and the 2026 IT Rules on AI-generated content.
quiz.explanation: Mirrors the UK's sector-led model rather than the EU's single-law approach.

quiz.question: What is FREE-AI?
quiz.answer: RBI's August 2025 framework: 7 sutras, 6 pillars, 26 recommendations — including a board-approved AI policy, an AI audit framework, and incident reporting. These are recommendations, not yet binding directions.
quiz.explanation: Expect RBI to turn parts of this into binding guidance over time — it's not law yet.

quiz.question: Name the six FREE-AI pillars.
quiz.answer: Infrastructure, Policy, Capacity (these enable innovation); Governance, Protection, Assurance (these mitigate risk).
quiz.explanation: The pillars deliberately split evenly between enabling AI adoption and controlling its risk.

quiz.question: What did India's 2026 IT Rules amendment change?
quiz.answer: AI-generated content must be labelled and carry provenance metadata, and certain takedowns must happen within 3 hours.
quiz.explanation: This is India's closest equivalent to the EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency duties.

quiz.question: Does the EU AI Act apply to an Indian bank with no EU office?
options: Yes, if its AI outputs are used in the EU
No, it only applies to EU-based companies
quiz.answer: Yes, if its AI outputs are used in the EU
quiz.explanation: The EU AI Act has extraterritorial reach — e.g. credit-scoring EU customers from anywhere in the world triggers it.

quiz.question: How would you advise a client operating across multiple regulatory regimes?
quiz.answer: Map the footprint and triggers, build one control set to the highest common standard with local overlays, map each control to every regime it satisfies, and set up ongoing horizon scanning for regulatory change.
quiz.explanation: This avoids running separate, duplicative compliance programmes per jurisdiction.

stops.artifactPrompt: Record yourself answering 3 of these questions out loud, unscripted, in under 30 seconds each.

stops.title: Self-check
stops.contentMd:
## Self-check

Answer out loud before reading the answers.

1. Name the UK's five AI principles.
2. Which UK regulator applies the Consumer Duty, and which applies SS1/23?
3. How many sutras, pillars and recommendations does FREE-AI have?
4. Is FREE-AI binding?
5. Why might an Indian bank be in scope of the EU AI Act?

**Answers:** (1) Safety, security and robustness; transparency and explainability; fairness; accountability and governance; contestability and redress. (2) FCA; PRA. (3) 7, 6, 26. (4) No: recommendations, which RBI may turn into guidance. (5) If its AI outputs are used in the EU, such as credit scoring of EU customers.

quiz.question: Name the UK's five AI principles.
quiz.answer: Safety, security and robustness; transparency and explainability; fairness; accountability and governance; contestability and redress.
quiz.explanation: From the 2023 white paper — not law, but the shared framework regulators apply within their existing powers.

quiz.question: Which UK regulator applies the Consumer Duty, and which applies SS1/23?
quiz.answer: The FCA applies the Consumer Duty. The PRA applies SS1/23.
quiz.explanation: Two different regulators with two different focuses — conduct/outcomes vs. prudential model risk.

quiz.question: How many sutras, pillars, and recommendations does RBI's FREE-AI framework have?
quiz.explanation: A common structural question to test whether you actually know the framework vs. just its name.

quiz.question: Is FREE-AI legally binding?
quiz.explanation: It's a set of recommendations for regulated entities, not binding directions — though RBI is expected to turn parts of it into guidance over time.

quiz.question: Why might an Indian bank with no EU presence still be in scope of the EU AI Act?
quiz.answer: If its AI outputs are used in the EU — for example, if it credit-scores EU customers — the Act's extraterritorial reach applies regardless of where the provider is based.
quiz.explanation: This is the same 'output used in the EU' trigger covered in the EU AI Act module.

stops.artifactPrompt: Write out your answers to all 5 self-check questions before revealing them. Note which ones you got wrong or hesitated on.
